paragraphs.text: Let your eyes settle somewhere in the room, somewhere they can rest for a little while, and notice the difference between looking for something and letting what is already there come into view. There is a surface beneath you. Notice where you meet it … the contact, the pressure, whatever you can actually feel. And while you notice that, a sound may reach you, or a breath may draw your attention, without needing you to arrange either one. You can give this a little time. A thought about the day may still be here. A thought about whether you’re doing this properly may be here too. There is room to notice a thought and return to the anchor you chose, without finishing the thought first. And as you return, you may find one detail that holds your interest … something about the sound, or the contact, or that particular way of listening … and let attention stay with it long enough to become curious. Perhaps you can give yourself the time you would give someone you care about who has begun to speak and hasn’t yet found the words. You can remain nearby, listening, without finishing their sentence for them. Let your chosen phrase come to mind now. Say it as an invitation, and notice how it is received. As you continue, your eyes can close, soften, or stay open. Let that be a choice you make. Listening may deepen while a sound from the room remains available in the background. Count slowly from five to one. Give each number its own moment. Five. Notice your chosen anchor again. Four. Let attention gather around what you find. Three. Leave a little space after the words. Two. Listen into that space, without preparing an answer. One. Stay here for a moment. Bring your chosen concern lightly to mind, or remain with your wish for contact. Let it be present without rehearsing its whole story. What am I noticing now? Give the response time to take its own form. It might be a sensation, a few words, an image, a feeling, or an impulse to move. There may be nothing clear yet. Let the words become less important while you listen.

paragraphs.text: Neither response establishes its origin. A protective part needn’t reveal its fear quickly; a comforting response doesn’t prove an interpretation either. The useful question is whether this way of responding helps you become clearer, steadier, and less hooked. Love and boundaries don’t require a verdict first.

paragraphs.text: Preview the sequence, choose one purpose, and decide whether you want to begin. Each family can be light, eyes-open, or replaced by no-trance contact. Notice the actual response—including no change—and let it determine the next move. Move, imagine, change the sensory channel, remain still, or stop. Use the complete waking return after every induction.

paragraphs.text: Feel the support beneath you and the position of one hand or foot. Press gently, stretch slightly, and release—or imagine it. Notice ease, tension, warmth, breath, or no change. Repeat with no more than three areas, letting “release” guide the sequence. Which area or inner voice wants attention? What support is needed? Restore ordinary movement and return.

paragraphs.text: Notice where your weight is carried. Let support carry 1% more effort, as if floating without losing contact, or keep ordinary weight and pressure. Notice the response. You may deliberately alternate attention toward ordinary awareness on the inhale and support on the exhale; name this fractionation beforehand. What becomes easier to hear? Keep the support, regain chosen weight and firm contact, then return.

paragraphs.text: Accompany a natural rhythm: breath, a comfortable hum, a finger tap, outside sound, or silent counting. No rhythm is also an option. Repeat “here, and here again,” noticing where attention lands between repetitions. Stop the deliberate rhythm and notice the first quiet beat, without trying to become blank. Is a word, feeling, need, or action clearer? Let ordinary rhythm resume and return.

paragraphs.text: Notice a concern with several strands. Imagine yarn unwinding, bubbles settling, or knots placed visibly beside you. Leave the object unchanged or label it in words when that fits better. Count only strands you actually set down; nothing is erased. Which needs warmth, protection, or action? Keep one useful strand, give the others a visible holding place, and return.

paragraphs.text: Hear the actual room and feel the body before imagining a step toward a chosen destination. Use footsteps, textures, or landmarks to gather attention. Change scenery or skip directly to dialogue when useful. Notice a detail without assigning hidden meaning; the mystery is how the scene develops, not what will be done to you. Who or what needs to speak? Return by the same route and close the imagined space.

paragraphs.text: Start with a small neutral area and what is already there. Imagine warmth, steadiness, or attention spreading to the next comfortable area, or keep it localized. Pause at each step and notice what changes without claiming medical repair. Does the body want contact, space, words, or ordinary care? Let the image recede, feel the whole body and real contact points, and return.

paragraphs.text: Prepare time, a place, tools, and boundaries for patient care. Let a signal, feeling, or younger state approach only as closely as welcome; choose language that doesn’t make you feel fragmented. Ask before responding, wait, reconnect only where welcome, rest, and reassess. An available inner adult or one borrowed function can help; you choose words, pace, and action. Aim for “good as you,” not erased history. Close the workspace, affirm wholeness and adult presence, and return.

paragraphs.text: Choose qualities you understand: warmth, boundary, steadiness, curiosity, or dignity. Imagine posture, voice, or attention with 1% more access to one quality. Observe rather than embody it when preferred. Notice a movement, word, image, or no response. Repeat to strengthen access, not replace identity. How would that quality meet today’s situation? Keep the quality and one useful action, release the role, affirm “I am myself,” and return.

paragraphs.text: Maggie Phillips and Claire Frederick, Healing the Divided Self (1995), especially pp.24–27, 45–50, and 83–90, discusses interactive hypnosis, sensory learning, self-hypnosis, and a definite return. It is a professional clinical book, not a self-help manual; its case procedures and historical claims shouldn’t be imported wholesale into solo practice. Adam Eason and Benjamin Parris’s ISH article on self-hypnosis discusses self-directed learning and its relationship to another hypnotist and recordings.
